title: Debug with a Failing Test
subtitle: A boundary regression in the order validator
learningObjective: Use a failing boundary test to verify a proposed cause, then prove the correction with the same runner.

productionNotes.setting: Synthetic training issue and Python checkout, viewed from VS Code. Run terminal actions in the approved workspace.
productionNotes.capture: Use the actual terminal recordings, source files and diff from the training fixture. Plan and Agent prompts are examples the learner can use.
productionNotes.direction: Teach one engineer seated beside you. Leave a beat after an invitation to predict. Read the meaning of a code expression. The screen carries its exact spelling.

sources.label: Python documentation · Test discovery and assertions
sources.use: Test discovery, assertFalse, and interpreting assertion failures.

sources.use: A reproducible red and green loop with Copilot in VS Code.

scenes.title: Three tests pass
scenes.narration: An order went through with zero items. The ticket says the smallest valid order is one. Open the training checkout in Visual Studio Code, with its terminal connected to the approved workspace. Run the command on screen from the directory containing the validator and its tests. Keep that command handy. We will use exactly the same one twice more. Three tests pass. Read their names with me. They try five, one, and negative one. Which test would catch an order for zero items?
scenes.action: Run the starting suite and read the test names.
scenes.focus: The three passing cases exercise five, one and negative one.
scenes.result: 3 tests passed on the starting checkout.
scenes.voiceDirection: Start in the middle of a real review. Let the last sentence invite curiosity.

scenes.title: Call the validator with zero
scenes.narration: Try the missing value directly. Import the same public function that the tests use. Call it with zero and print the return value. There it is. True. Read the ticket beside that result. An order with zero items must be rejected, so we expected false. The existing tests can all pass while this particular call gives the wrong answer. Leave the source as it is for a moment. This is our chance to find out whether a new test can actually detect the defect.
scenes.action: Run a single read-only call. Compare the returned value with the ticket.
scenes.focus: A call with zero returns True on the original source.
scenes.result: Observed True. The issue requires False.
scenes.voiceDirection: Slow enough to hear the difference between the observation and the requirement.

scenes.title: Predict what the comparison does
scenes.narration: Here is a question you can put to Copilot in Plan mode. Which expression admits zero, and what will happen if we assert that zero must be rejected? Include the issue, the validator, and its tests. Check the prediction yourself on line three. Substitute zero for quantity. Is zero greater than or equal to zero? Yes. The equality part is enough to let it through. Now try one and negative one in your head. One is greater than zero. Negative one is smaller. The equality at the boundary explains all three outcomes.
scenes.action: Ask Plan for a prediction, then evaluate the actual source line.
scenes.focus: Equality makes the original expression true at exactly zero.
scenes.code:
Plan prompt: Read the issue, validator, and tests. Which expression admits zero? Predict the assertion outcome before proposing edits.
return quantity >= 0
scenes.result: At zero, the original comparison evaluates to True.
scenes.voiceDirection: Sound like someone thinking at the reader’s elbow. Give the equality a little space.

beats.text: Here is a question you can put to Copilot in Plan mode. Which expression admits zero, and what will happen if we assert that zero must be rejected? Include the issue, the validator, and its tests.
beats.shot: Show an editable Plan prompt with the three pieces of context. Label the prompt as an example, then cut to actual source.
beats.voiceDirection: Read the question in one connected phrase.

beats.text: Check the prediction yourself on line three. Substitute zero for quantity. Is zero greater than or equal to zero? Yes. The equality part is enough to let it through.
beats.shot: Substitute the probe value over quantity in the captured original expression. Isolate the equality stroke while the full operator stays legible.
beats.voiceDirection: Leave room for the learner to answer.

beats.text: Now try one and negative one in your head. One is greater than zero. Negative one is smaller. The equality at the boundary explains all three outcomes.
beats.shot: Mark each original comparison explicitly. Negative one returns False, zero returns True, and one returns True.
beats.voiceDirection: Warm, deliberate explanation.

scenes.title: Add the test first
scenes.narration: Give Agent a small first job. Add one zero regression to the existing test class and leave the validator untouched. You can also type the two lines shown here. Read the assertion from the inside out. The function receives zero. The assertion requires its result to be false. A test that simply checks whether zero is false would tell us nothing about our validator. Before running it, inspect the changed file list. You should see the test file alone. That lets us attribute the next failure to the behavior already present in the starting code.
scenes.action: Ask Agent for one regression and inspect the test-only diff.
scenes.focus: The added assertion calls the public function with zero and expects False.
scenes.result: Only tests/test_order_quantity.py changes at this step.
scenes.voiceDirection: Read the intention behind the assertion. Let the viewer inspect the diff.

beats.voiceDirection: Conversational request, then a short breath.

beats.voiceDirection: Small emphasis on our validator.

beats.voiceDirection: Even and precise.

scenes.title: Find the intended failure
scenes.narration: Run the same command again. First check the total. Four tests ran this time. Now find the failure and follow it back to the line that calls the validator with zero. Read the assertion message. True is not false. That is the observation we predicted. The three earlier cases still pass. Keep this output with the test-only patch. Suppose the runner had stopped at an import error. What would you know about zero? Very little. Fix the setup and rerun until the assertion itself executes.
scenes.action: Rerun the baseline command and locate the failing assertion.
scenes.focus: The newly discovered fourth test executes and fails for the expected reason.
scenes.result:
test_rejects_zero ... FAIL
AssertionError: True is not false
Ran 4 tests. FAILED (failures=1)
scenes.voiceDirection: Keep the failure reassuring. It supplies evidence.

scenes.title: Remove the equality
scenes.narration: Now the regression can catch the bug. Open the production diff. Remove the equals sign. The expression now asks whether quantity is strictly greater than zero. Keep the public function signature and the new assertion as they are. Make a prediction before the next run. Zero is equal to zero, so the new expression returns false. Five and one should still pass. Negative one should still be rejected.
scenes.action: Change the boundary operator and keep the test and signature intact.
scenes.focus: Removing the equality changes the outcome at zero.
scenes.result: The fix changes one comparison in order_quantity.py.
scenes.voiceDirection: Small movement, plain delivery. Let the change be visually obvious.

beats.text: Now the regression can catch the bug. Open the production diff. Remove the equals sign. The expression now asks whether quantity is strictly greater than zero. Keep the public function signature and the new assertion as they are.
beats.shot: Show the real red-to-green source diff. Magnify only the changing operator, then restore the surrounding function.
beats.voiceDirection: Stress strictly once.

beats.text: Make a prediction before the next run. Zero is equal to zero, so the new expression returns false. Five and one should still pass. Negative one should still be rejected.
beats.shot: Drive zero through before and after expressions, then briefly show the neighbor values unchanged. Do not show the final run output yet.
beats.voiceDirection: Let the learner anticipate each result.

scenes.title: Replay the same four tests
scenes.narration: Run that saved command a third time. The zero test now passes, and the total is still four. Compare the failure and the pass side by side. The method name and its assertion are identical. For a handoff, give your teammate the starting checkout, the test-only diff and its failing output, then the source diff and its passing output. They can apply the changes in that order and repeat your result.
scenes.action: Verify the passing zero test and the three original cases.
scenes.focus: The regression switches from FAIL to ok with its assertion unchanged.
scenes.voiceDirection: Release the tension at the passing run. Stay exact about what the evidence covers.

scenes.title: Try a boundary at the other end
scenes.narration: Try the same method on a separate exercise. An order may contain one through one hundred items, including one hundred. The draft on screen uses a strict comparison at each end. Pause the video here. Write the expected answers for ninety-nine, one hundred, and one hundred and one. Which single regression would expose the mistake before you edit the function? Ready? The answers are true, true, and false. The draft rejects exactly one of those valid examples, one hundred. Write an assertion that accepts one hundred. Watch it fail, then include equality at the upper limit and rerun. Notice how the ticket decided which way equality belongs. Reading the rule, testing the edge, and replaying the same check will serve you at either end of a range.
scenes.action: Pause and predict the outputs for 99, 100 and 101.
scenes.focus: A new inclusive maximum reveals a different equality error.
scenes.code:
Practice only: accept integers from 1 through 100.
Starting expression: 0 < quantity < 100
Probe 99, 100, 101. Write the equality regression.
scenes.result: Expected True, True, False. The original exercise expression rejects 100. Fix the upper comparison to <=.
scenes.voiceDirection: Leave a genuine work pause after the prompt. Let the reveal feel like checking together.

beats.shot: End with the rule and the single input that discriminates between the two expressions. Leave the original patch readily distinguishable.
beats.voiceDirection: Gentle finish.
